Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Expectation2: Arrive at the polling station during designated voting hours
Situation2: Polls stay open all day and the voter has a light schedule.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was about to head out the door. It was Jamie, my closest friend, and I could hear the strain in their voice before they even finished saying hello. “Can you talk? I really need someone right now,” Jamie said, voice trembling. I knew what was expected of me—I’ve always been the one to listen, to offer comfort when things got rough. But today was also Election Day, and I’d promised myself I’d vote before noon, just to get it done. The polling station was only a few blocks away, and with my light schedule, I could technically go anytime. Still, I felt a knot tighten in my stomach. Jamie needed me, but I also felt the weight of my civic duty, the importance of showing up and making my voice heard. I could hear Jamie sniffling softly on the other end, waiting for me to say something, and I stood there, keys in hand, torn between being the friend they needed and the responsible voter I wanted to be.
